## Proof

We prove the inequality for strictly positive $a_i, b_i$; the general nonnegative case follows by continuity (both sides are continuous functions of the $2n$ variables, and $(0,\infty)^{2n}$ is dense in $[0,\infty)^{2n}$).

**Step 1 — Reduction to a kernel inequality.**

Assume $a_i, b_i > 0$. Set $x_i = a_i/b_i > 0$ and $c_i = b_i > 0$. Then for every pair $(i,j)$,

$$\min(a_i a_j,\, b_i b_j) = c_i c_j \min(x_i x_j,\,1), \qquad \min(a_i b_j,\, a_j b_i) = c_i c_j \min(x_i,\,x_j).$$

So the desired inequality is equivalent to

$$\sum_{i,j} c_i c_j\,\min(x_i x_j,1)\;\le\;\sum_{i,j} c_i c_j\,\min(x_i,x_j). \tag{1}$$

Now write $x_i = e^{v_i}$ with $v_i\in\mathbb{R}$, and set $w_i = c_i\,e^{v_i/2} = c_i\sqrt{x_i} = \sqrt{a_i b_i} > 0$. Using
$$\min(e^s,1)=e^{s/2}\,e^{-|s|/2}, \qquad \min(e^{v_i},e^{v_j})=e^{(v_i+v_j)/2}\,e^{-|v_i-v_j|/2},$$
and defining $g(t):=e^{-|t|/2}$, identity (1) becomes

$$\sum_{i,j} w_i w_j\, g(v_i+v_j)\;\le\;\sum_{i,j} w_i w_j\, g(v_i-v_j). \tag{2}$$

Equivalently, with $A_{ij}=g(v_i-v_j)$ and $B_{ij}=g(v_i+v_j)$, we must show $\mathbf{w}^{\mathsf T}(A-B)\mathbf{w}\ge 0$.

**Step 2 — Positive definiteness of $g$.**

The function $g(t)=e^{-|t|/2}$ admits the Fourier representation

$$g(t)=e^{-|t|/2}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ist}}{s^2+\tfrac14}\,ds.$$

Hence for any real points $t_1,\dots,t_m$ and any real $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m$,

$$\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j\,g(t_i-t_j)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\bigl|\sum_i \alpha_i e^{ist_i}\bigr|^2}{s^2+\tfrac14}\,ds\;\ge\;0.$$

So $g$ is **positive definite**: every matrix $[g(t_i-t_j)]$ is positive semidefinite (PSD).

**Step 3 — $A-B$ is positive semidefinite.**

Consider the $2n$ points $v_1,\dots,v_n,-v_1,\dots,-v_n$. By positive definiteness of $g$, the $2n\times 2n$ Gram matrix

$$K=\bigl[\,g(p_r-p_s)\,\bigr]_{r,s=1}^{2n},\qquad (p_1,\dots,p_{2n})=(v_1,\dots,v_n,-v_1,\dots,-v_n)$$

is PSD. Since $g$ is even, $K$ has the block form

$$K=\begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ B & A \end{pmatrix},\qquad A_{ij}=g(v_i-v_j),\;\; B_{ij}=g(v_i+v_j).$$

For any $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^n$, apply the vector $u=(\alpha,-\alpha)\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}$:

$$0\le u^{\mathsf T}Ku = \alpha^{\mathsf T}A\alpha - \alpha^{\mathsf T}B\alpha - \alpha^{\mathsf T}B\alpha + \alpha^{\mathsf T}A\alpha = 2\,\alpha^{\mathsf T}(A-B)\alpha.$$

Thus $\alpha^{\mathsf T}(A-B)\alpha\ge 0$ for **all** real $\alpha$; i.e. $A-B$ is PSD.

**Step 4 — Conclusion.**

Since $A-B$ is PSD and $\mathbf{w}=(w_1,\dots,w_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n$,

$$\sum_{i,j}w_i w_j\bigl[g(v_i-v_j)-g(v_i+v_j)\bigr]=\mathbf{w}^{\mathsf T}(A-B)\mathbf{w}\;\ge\;0,$$

which is exactly (2). Tracing back through Step 1 yields

$$\sum_{i,j}\min(a_i a_j,\,b_i b_j)\;\le\;\sum_{i,j}\min(a_i b_j,\,a_j b_i)$$

for all positive $a_i,b_i$, and by continuity for all nonnegative $a_i,b_i$. $\blacksquare$

## Proof

We prove the inequality for strictly positive $a_i, b_i$; the general nonnegative case follows by continuity (both sides are continuous functions of the $2n$ variables, and $(0,\infty)^{2n}$ is dense in $[0,\infty)^{2n}$).

**Step 1 — Reduction to a kernel inequality.**

Assume $a_i, b_i > 0$. Set $x_i = a_i/b_i > 0$ and $c_i = b_i > 0$. Then for every pair $(i,j)$,

$$\min(a_i a_j,\, b_i b_j) = c_i c_j \min(x_i x_j,\,1), \qquad \min(a_i b_j,\, a_j b_i) = c_i c_j \min(x_i,\,x_j).$$

So the desired inequality is equivalent to

$$\sum_{i,j} c_i c_j\,\min(x_i x_j,1)\;\le\;\sum_{i,j} c_i c_j\,\min(x_i,x_j). \tag{1}$$

Now write $x_i = e^{v_i}$ with $v_i\in\mathbb{R}$, and set $w_i = c_i\,e^{v_i/2} = c_i\sqrt{x_i} = \sqrt{a_i b_i} > 0$. Using
$$\min(e^s,1)=e^{s/2}\,e^{-|s|/2}, \qquad \min(e^{v_i},e^{v_j})=e^{(v_i+v_j)/2}\,e^{-|v_i-v_j|/2},$$
and defining $g(t):=e^{-|t|/2}$, identity (1) becomes

$$\sum_{i,j} w_i w_j\, g(v_i+v_j)\;\le\;\sum_{i,j} w_i w_j\, g(v_i-v_j). \tag{2}$$

Equivalently, with $A_{ij}=g(v_i-v_j)$ and $B_{ij}=g(v_i+v_j)$, we must show $\mathbf{w}^{\mathsf T}(A-B)\mathbf{w}\ge 0$.

**Step 2 — Positive definiteness of $g$.**

The function $g(t)=e^{-|t|/2}$ admits the Fourier representation

$$g(t)=e^{-|t|/2}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ist}}{s^2+\tfrac14}\,ds.$$

Hence for any real points $t_1,\dots,t_m$ and any real $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m$,

$$\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j\,g(t_i-t_j)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\bigl|\sum_i \alpha_i e^{ist_i}\bigr|^2}{s^2+\tfrac14}\,ds\;\ge\;0.$$

So $g$ is **positive definite**: every matrix $[g(t_i-t_j)]$ is positive semidefinite (PSD).

**Step 3 — $A-B$ is positive semidefinite.**

Consider the $2n$ points $v_1,\dots,v_n,-v_1,\dots,-v_n$. By positive definiteness of $g$, the $2n\times 2n$ Gram matrix

$$K=\bigl[\,g(p_r-p_s)\,\bigr]_{r,s=1}^{2n},\qquad (p_1,\dots,p_{2n})=(v_1,\dots,v_n,-v_1,\dots,-v_n)$$

is PSD. Since $g$ is even, $K$ has the block form

$$K=\begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ B & A \end{pmatrix},\qquad A_{ij}=g(v_i-v_j),\;\; B_{ij}=g(v_i+v_j).$$

For any $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^n$, apply the vector $u=(\alpha,-\alpha)\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}$:

$$0\le u^{\mathsf T}Ku = \alpha^{\mathsf T}A\alpha - \alpha^{\mathsf T}B\alpha - \alpha^{\mathsf T}B\alpha + \alpha^{\mathsf T}A\alpha = 2\,\alpha^{\mathsf T}(A-B)\alpha.$$

Thus $\alpha^{\mathsf T}(A-B)\alpha\ge 0$ for **all** real $\alpha$; i.e. $A-B$ is PSD.

**Step 4 — Conclusion.**

Since $A-B$ is PSD and $\mathbf{w}=(w_1,\dots,w_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n$,

$$\sum_{i,j}w_i w_j\bigl[g(v_i-v_j)-g(v_i+v_j)\bigr]=\mathbf{w}^{\mathsf T}(A-B)\mathbf{w}\;\ge\;0,$$

which is exactly (2). Tracing back through Step 1 yields

$$\sum_{i,j}\min(a_i a_j,\,b_i b_j)\;\le\;\sum_{i,j}\min(a_i b_j,\,a_j b_i)$$

for all positive $a_i,b_i$, and by continuity for all nonnegative $a_i,b_i$. $\blacksquare$
